parts: Lesson 23: Life Processes – II: Control and Coordination — Summary

The nervous system (brain, spinal cord, sense organs and nerves) and the endocrine system (glands that pour chemical messengers called hormones directly into the blood) work together as a team to control and coordinate all our activities — physical actions, thinking and emotions. Eating, for example, involves seeing food, moving hands to the mouth, feeling full, and secreting digestive juices at the right time. A stimulus is any change that starts a response — touch, pressure, sound, light, heat, cold, chemicals.

The neuron (nerve cell) is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. Its dendrites (branched projections) receive impulses; the cell body has a nucleus and cytoplasm; the long axon (nerve fibre), covered by a fatty sheath with gaps called nodes of Ranvier, carries the impulse away and ends in bulbs that store chemicals called neurotransmitters. The junction between two neurons is a synapse, with a tiny gap, the synaptic cleft. When an impulse reaches the end of an axon, the neurotransmitter is released, crosses the cleft and starts an impulse in the next neuron, and finally in a muscle or gland. Types: sensory neurons carry impulses from receptors (sense organs) to the brain or spinal cord; motor neurons carry them from the brain or spinal cord to effectors (muscles or glands); association (connecting) neurons in the brain and spinal cord link the two.

A nerve is a bundle of axons in a sheath, like an electric cable with insulated wires. Sensory nerves bring impulses to the brain or spinal cord (optic nerve); motor nerves carry them to muscles or glands; mixed nerves contain both (spinal nerves). There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves (from the brain) and 31 pairs of spinal nerves (from the spinal cord).

The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord. The brain lies in the bony cranium and is covered by three meninges — the tough outer dura mater, the delicate web-like arachnoid and the inner, blood-rich pia mater. Cerebrospinal fluid between them cushions the brain against shocks. Meningitis is a contagious inflammation of the meninges caused by microbes (high fever, headache, stiff neck, sensitivity to light).

The cerebrum, the largest part, has two hemispheres with a folded grey cortex (cell bodies) over inner white matter (axons); it is the seat of intelligence, thinking, memory, reasoning, consciousness and will, and controls voluntary actions. The cerebellum, below the cerebrum, maintains balance and coordinates muscular movements (a drunk person walks clumsily because alcohol affects it). The medulla oblongata, at the base of the brain (part of the hind-brain), continues as the spinal cord and controls involuntary actions — heartbeat, breathing, peristalsis; injury to it can be fatal. The hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger and the pituitary.

The spinal cord runs from the medulla down the neural canal of the backbone, covered by the same three meninges. Its grey matter (cell bodies) is inside and white matter (axons) outside — the reverse of the brain — with a central canal of cerebrospinal fluid. Functions: (1) it controls reflex actions below the neck; (2) it carries sensory impulses from the skin and muscles to the brain; (3) it carries motor impulses from the brain to the muscles of the trunk and limbs.

A reflex action is a quick, automatic, involuntary response to a stimulus, controlled by the spinal cord without the involvement of the brain — withdrawing the hand from a hot object or a needle, closing the eyes in a dust storm, tears washing out dust, shivering in cold, sweating in heat. Natural (inborn) reflexes need no learning — breathing, swallowing, coughing, blinking. Conditioned (acquired) reflexes are learnt from experience, e.g. the mouth watering at the smell of favourite food; they fade unless reinforced. The path of a reflex is the reflex arc: stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → spinal cord (association neuron) → motor neuron → effector (muscle or gland) → response.

The peripheral nervous system (PNS) connects the CNS with the rest of the body. Its somatic part (cranial and spinal nerves) controls voluntary actions of skeletal muscles. Its autonomic part, chains of nerves and ganglia beside the backbone, controls involuntary actions of internal organs: the sympathetic system prepares the body for stress ('fight or flight' with adrenaline) — faster heartbeat, dilated pupils, sugar released from the liver; the parasympathetic system restores normal conditions — saliva and tears, digestion. The two are complementary.

A hormone is a chemical secreted by an endocrine gland and carried by the blood to a target organ elsewhere, where it causes a specific effect; too much or too little causes disease. Pituitary (at the base of the brain): growth hormone — too little causes dwarfism, too much gigantism; gonad-stimulating hormones make the ovaries produce oestrogen and progesterone and the testes produce testosterone at puberty, bringing secondary sexual characters; hyperactivity causes Cushing's disease. Thyroid (in the neck): its hormone (thyroxine) controls the rate of metabolism, growth and development — overactivity is hyperthyroidism, underactivity hypothyroidism; cretinism is severely stunted physical and mental growth from thyroid deficiency; simple goitre (swelling of the neck) is caused by lack of iodine, prevented by iodised salt. Pancreas: insulin and glucagon control blood glucose; too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus. Adrenal glands secrete adrenaline in emergencies; ovaries and testes secrete sex hormones.
